title: Jannik Sinner reclaims world No. 1 after Monte Carlo Masters win over Carlos Alcaraz
content:
After just over an hour of wild serves, erratic groundstrokes and uncharacteristic misses at both ends of Court Rainier III, the first set of the first meeting between Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner in 2026 had an appropriate ending: A very strange tiebreak.

At 2-2, with the space for an inside-in forehand approach beckoning, Alcaraz hit an inside-out forehand drop shot right to the easiest spot on the court for Sinner to get it. The Italian flicked the ball away for a winner, and took control. But on his first set point, he smacked a forehand into the net.

It didn’t matter, as Alcaraz sent a second serve long, and Sinner claimed the first set of an absorbing but uneven Monte Carlo Masters final defined by the wind swirling around the French Riviera.

When it was over, Sinner had reclaimed the world No. 1 ranking with a 7-6(5), 6-3 win that is unlikely to teach either man about the rest of their clay season, but will give Sinner a boost in his aim to wrestle the French Open from his nearest rival — and with it, complete the career Grand Slam, as Alcaraz did at this year’s Australian Open.

“Getting back to No. 1 means a lot, but the ranking is secondary,” the Italian said after winning his first clay title at Grand Slam or ATP Masters 1000 level.

Alcaraz led by a break in each set, but he failed to punish Sinner’s first serve going awry in the opener, and then found himself struggling to convert when in need of breathing room. Across nine service games in which he got to 40, Alcaraz won the game at the first opportunity just three times; Sinner went six from 10, and found six of six first serves in the tiebreak, where Alcaraz made just two.

Alcaraz inevitably produced one moment of the magic only he has — scampering out from his backhand corner to dig a forehand down the line and break Sinner’s serve early in the second set — but his inability to produce separation behind his serve when he had an advantage continually stalled his momentum.

Sinner also successfully biased the match in his direction, running around his forehand more often than normal and denying Alcaraz the opportunity to hit his own. Sinner played 117 forehands to 98 for Alcaraz, and 80 backhands to 112.

With his fourth consecutive ATP Masters 1000 title, Sinner ties a record held by Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic; with his second win over Alcaraz on clay, he moves his overall head-to-head record against the Spaniard to 7-10.

Sinner will skip the next tournament week, while Alcaraz is scheduled to play the Barcelona Open. The gap between them at the top of the world rankings come Monday will be 110 points; Alexander Zverev, at world No. 3, is almost 7,700 points behind Alcaraz at world No. 2.
